states.name: selected
states.note: Set with the selected prop.

states.name: empty
states.note: Set with the empty prop.

components.summary: A gallery of images in even rows that adjusts to the screen, with optional selecting and an empty message.
components.description: MediaGrid lays out images with the same spacing and the same shape. It uses 2 columns on small screens, 3 on medium and 4 on large, up to the limit you set. Selecting is optional, with a checkbox button on each image. With no images, it shows an empty message.
components.purpose: Lays out many images in even rows with one gap and one shape, so they are easy to scan. It can let people pick several, and shows an empty message when there is nothing.
useFor: A gallery of uploads or generated images.
Picking several images to download, delete or reuse: turn on selectable.

notFor.text: Picking one of several AI-made options
A single image

whenToUse: Give the grid a name that says what the images are.
Use one shape for the whole grid.
Replace the empty message when you know the reason, such as a filter.
avoid: Do not mix shapes in one grid.
Do not show what is chosen with color alone. The check mark does that.
Do not use it for a single image. Use MediaFrame.
accessibility: The grid is a named list, so screen readers say how many images there are.
Each select button is a checkbox named "Select" plus the image description. It works with Tab, Enter and Space.
A chosen image shows a check mark and a ring, not just color.
The count line is announced and updates when the choice changes.
accessibilityYouDo: Give the grid a label that says what the images are, such as "Your uploads".
Write a description for every image. A decorative image's select button is named only by its id.
onPhone: The grid is two columns on a phone, and three or four only from the md and xl breakpoints.
In select mode, each check button sits in the top right corner of the image. On touch screens it keeps its 28px size and has a 44px by 44px tap area.
The count line is 12px text above the grid, and it is announced as a status when the count changes.

props.name: items
props.description: Each item is the MediaFrame props except ratio and className, plus an id.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name of the list.

props.name: columns
props.description: Maximum columns. Fewer show on narrower screens.

props.name: ratio
props.description: Ratio shared by every tile.

props.name: selectable
props.description: Adds a checkbox button to each tile.

props.name: selected
props.description: Controlled selection as item ids.

props.name: onSelectedChange
props.description: Called with the new selection.

props.name: empty
props.description: Replaces the default EmptyState.

props.name: countLabel
props.description: Builds the count line. Defaults to a count of images and selected.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes for the wrapper.

components.name: AIMark
components.summary: A small four-point shape that tells people something was made by AI.
components.description: AIMark is a small shape that matches the color of the text beside it. By default it is just decoration. Give it a title and screen readers will read it out. Many people know the sparkle means AI, but not what the AI does. So add words whenever the action matters.
components.purpose: The one shape this system uses to mean AI. It takes the color of the text beside it, and its arms are slightly uneven, so it reads as our own mark rather than a generic sparkle.
useFor: Beside the words on a button that starts an AI action, like Summarize.
On its own, with a title, inside a small badge or circle.
Inside other AI labels that need a symbol.

notFor.text: Labelling a piece of content as made by AI
Explaining how AI content was made
Showing who wrote a message

whenToUse: Add words when the action is specific, like Summarize or Rewrite.
Use one mark for AI everywhere so people learn it.
Match its size to the text beside it.
Give it a title when it stands alone.
avoid: Put it alone on every button. Too many marks lose their meaning.
Use a second AI symbol in the same product.
Make it lime on a plain page background. Lime is a fill that holds dark text.
Use it as decoration where nothing is made by AI.
accessibility: Without a title, screen readers skip it and read only the words beside it.
With a title, screen readers read it as an image with that name.
It never takes keyboard focus.
accessibilityYouDo: Give it a title when it stands alone, so screen readers can say what it means.
Check that it stands out from its background when alone. It copies the text color.
Keep a button around it at least 24 pixels wide.
onPhone: The mark is a fixed pixel size and looks the same on a phone.
It is not tappable. Put it inside a button if it starts something, and that button gets a 44px target on touch screens.

props.name: size
props.description: Pixel size of the square mark.

props.name: title
props.description: Accessible name. When set the mark has role img and this label. When omitted it is hidden from assistive technology.

props.name: ...svg props
props.description: Other props go to the svg element, except width, height and title.

examples.title: Sizes
examples.description: Five sizes. The first three match small, medium and large text. The last two are for use on their own.

examples.title: Paired with text
examples.description: The mark sits beside words that say what will happen. A screen reader reads only the words.
examples.code: <Button variant="secondary"><AIMark size={16} />Summarize this page</Button>

examples.title: Named image
examples.description: When the mark stands alone, give it a title so screen readers can say what it means.

components.name: AIPresence

states.name: status
states.note: Set with the state prop.

components.summary: A moving orb that shows whether the assistant is waiting, listening, thinking, speaking, or has hit a problem.
components.description: AIPresence is a small dark glass lens set in a fine bezel, with lime light inside it and the AI mark at its heart, under a soft glow. Each state moves differently: Ready breathes slowly, Listening sends rings outward, Thinking circles a comet of light inside the rim, Speaking pulses with the voice, and an error dims the light to red. When the state changes, it glides smoothly to the new look. The state is always written out in words too. For people who turn off motion, it stays still and switches instantly. It is not a button, so place a labelled Stop button next to it.
components.purpose: A drawn orb that shows what a voice assistant is doing: waiting, listening, thinking, speaking or stuck. It glides between states instead of restarting, and the state is always given in words too.
useFor: A voice conversation, to show whether the assistant is listening or speaking.
The pause while the assistant thinks between voice turns.
Reacting to how loud the speaker is: pass level.

notFor.text: Showing who wrote a message
A whole voice screen with its controls
The wait before a text reply

whenToUse: Place a labelled Stop button beside the orb whenever the person can interrupt.
Ask for microphone permission when the person presses a button, then start the orb.
Keep the label showing unless the state is written out nearby.
Pass the raw volume and let the orb smooth it.
avoid: Make the orb the only button or the only sign of what is happening.
Change the state many times a second. Screen readers announce only real changes.
Use amber for the problem state. Amber is only for when a person has to act.
Add a glow outside the disc, or use rainbow or purple gradients.
accessibility: Screen readers hear the state in words, politely, each time it changes.
The drawing is hidden from screen readers.
For people who turn off motion, the orb stays still, ignores volume and changes state instantly.
The problem state shows the words "Something went wrong", not only a red center.
accessibilityYouDo: Put a labelled Stop button next to it whenever people can interrupt. The orb is not a button.
Change state only when the assistant really changes what it is doing. Screen readers hear each change.
Keep the visible label on, unless the state is written out nearby.
onPhone: The orb is a fixed size (32, 64 or 112px) and does not scale with the screen, so pick the size that fits a narrow screen.
The orb and its label sit on one row, so a long label can squeeze a small screen. Keep the label short.
It is not a control. Place a Stop button beside it, which has a 44px tap area on touch screens.
Under reduced motion it draws a still frame instead of the animation.

props.name: state
props.description: Current state. Each state is a row of animation targets.

props.name: size
props.description: 32, 64 or 112 pixels.

props.name: level
props.description: Audio amplitude from 0 to 1. Smoothed inside the component. Ignored under reduced motion.

props.name: showLabel
props.description: Show the state as visible text. The status region is present either way.

props.name: labels
props.description: Replace the text for any state.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes for the wrapper.

examples.title: Switch between states
examples.description: The orb glides between states. The label and the hidden message for screen readers change only when the state does.

examples.title: Audio level
examples.description: Pass the sound volume from 0 to 1. The orb smooths it, rising fast and falling slowly.
examples.code: <AIPresence state="speaking" size="lg" level={level} />

examples.title: Sizes
examples.code:
<AIPresence size="sm" state="thinking" />
<AIPresence size="md" state="thinking" />
<AIPresence size="lg" state="thinking" showLabel={false} />

components.name: AILabel

states.name: hover
states.note: The lime pill darkens slightly under the pointer.

states.name: focus
states.note: A visible focus ring appears on the label button on keyboard focus.

states.name: open
states.note: Pressing the label opens a popover with the overview, details, resources and actions you pass, or a default line if none are passed.

states.name: edited
states.note: Pass edited to replace the pill with a small revert button that calls onRevert.

states.name: placed
states.note: Pass placed to pin the label to a corner or edge of its parent, depending on level.

components.summary: A small lime tag that says content was made by AI and explains how. Once a person edits the content, it becomes an undo button.
components.description: AILabel marks content as made by AI. Pressing it opens a small note with up to four parts: overview, details, links and buttons. It only labels and explains. It never starts AI work. The level setting picks where it sits: on a feature, a message, a field or an image. After an edit, the lime color goes away and an icon button brings back the AI version.
components.purpose: A small lime tag that marks content as made by AI and opens a note explaining how. Once a person edits the content it turns into an undo button, because the content is no longer purely AI.
useFor: A box, message, field or image whose content the AI made.
Explaining what the AI did, with details, links or buttons.
Letting people go back to the AI version after they edit it.

notFor.text: A button that starts AI work
A simple mark with no explanation
A full record of where content came from

whenToUse: Put one label on the whole box, not one on every line.
Keep the label away from the edge of the box.
Use the buttons part for things like Learn more or Turn off.
Set edited to true as soon as a person changes the content, so the undo button appears.
In onRevert, restore the AI version and set edited back to false.
avoid: Use the label as a button that starts AI work.
Put it on content a person wrote.
Make the label amber. Amber is only for when a person has to act.
Push the label right up against the edge of a box.
accessibility: The tag is a real button. Screen readers hear its words, then "About this AI content", and whether the note is open.
Opening the note moves the keyboard into it. Escape closes it and returns the keyboard to the tag; tabbing away or clicking outside also closes it.
Each part of the note is named, such as Overview and Details.
The undo button shows only an icon, but screen readers hear "Revert to AI version".
The pressable area is at least 24 pixels tall, and 44 on touch screens.
accessibilityYouDo: Give buttons and links you put in the note their own clear words.
onPhone: On touch screens the pill keeps its size and has a 44px tap area. The revert button grows to 44px square.
The explainer opens on tap and closes by tapping outside, and its panel is at most the screen width minus 2rem.
Buttons in the Actions section wrap onto more lines on a narrow screen.

props.name: level
props.description: Where the label sits. Feature is the upper right of a container. Field is the right side, vertically centred. Message and image are our own placements.

props.name: size
props.description: Pill and mark size. Match the adjacent text size.

props.name: text
props.description: Word in the pill.

props.name: placed
props.description: Apply absolute placement for the level. The parent must be positioned.

props.name: overview
props.description: Toggletip section: what the AI did.

props.name: details
props.description: Toggletip section: specifics for this instance.

props.name: resources
props.description: Toggletip section: links.

props.name: actions
props.description: Toggletip section: buttons. The label itself never triggers AI work.

props.name: edited
props.description: Drops the tint and shows the icon-only revert button.

props.name: onRevert
props.description: Called when revert is pressed. The app restores the AI version.

props.name: revertLabel
props.description: Accessible name of the revert button.

props.name: popoverLabel
props.description: Accessible name of the toggletip panel.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes for the wrapper.

examples.title: Feature container
examples.description: Sits at the upper right of a box, a little away from the edge.

examples.title: Toggletip sections
examples.description: All four parts filled in. Buttons are plain buttons and links are links. Escape or a click outside closes the note.

examples.title: Edited, with revert
examples.description: After an edit, the tag turns into an icon button named Revert to AI version. Pressing it brings the tag back.

examples.title: Sizes
examples.description: Match the size to the text around it.

components.name: ChartFrame

states.name: status
states.note: Set with the state prop.

states.name: empty
states.note: Set with the empty prop.

components.summary: The box every chart sits in. It adds a title, a short written summary, a table view and clear messages when data is loading or missing.
components.description: ChartFrame gives a chart a title, a line saying what is measured and over what time, and a short summary in words. A View as table button swaps the chart for the same numbers in a table. It also shows messages while data loads, when there is none, or when something fails. In a very narrow space it shows a tiny trend line instead.
components.purpose: The box every chart sits in. It puts the title, what is measured and a summary in words above the chart, so the point is clear before anyone reads the lines.
useFor: Any chart on a page, so it gets a title, a summary and a table view.
Showing clear messages while data loads, when there is none, or when loading fails.
A chart that may land in a narrow space: pass a small trend line as the fallback.

notFor.text: One headline number
A table of numbers with no chart

whenToUse: Write the summary as a sentence that says what the data shows, with the key number.
Say what is measured and over what time in the subtitle.
Give every chart a table, so the table button is always there.
When there is nothing to show, say why and what to do next.
Pass onRetry, so the error message offers a Try again button.
avoid: Don't skip the summary because the chart looks obvious. Some people need the words.
Don't hide numbers in a pop-up. Put them in the table.
Don't put filters inside the box. Keep them in one row above the charts they control.
Don't make the box shorter than the chart and its labels.
accessibility: The title and summary sit in the chart's caption, so screen readers hear them with the chart.
View as table swaps in a real table with the same numbers, and the button label changes to match the view.
While data loads, screen readers hear "Loading chart".
A failure is announced right away.
accessibilityYouDo: Write a summary that says what the data shows, with the key number. Some people only get the words.
Pass table data for every chart, or the View as table button does not appear.
onPhone: The chart is drawn at the width of the frame, and below minWidth (280px unless you change it) it is replaced by your fallback, usually a Sparkline, with a note to use the table view.
Cards use 16px padding and the title wraps instead of being cut off.
The View as table button swaps in a DataTable that scrolls sideways inside the frame, so give the table a narrow column set for phones.

props.name: title
props.description: Chart title, set in the display style.

props.name: subtitle
props.description: States the unit and the time window.

props.name: summary
props.description: Plain-language reading of the chart, shown above it in body text.

props.name: children
props.description: The chart. It receives the full width of the frame.

props.name: table
props.description: Data for the table view. Without it the toggle is hidden. Each chart exports a helper that builds it.

props.name: source
props.description: Source line shown under the chart.

props.name: note
props.description: Caveat shown after the source, for example that the latest point is still streaming.

props.name: legend
props.description: Rendered above the chart. Charts draw their own legend, so use this only for a shared legend.

props.name: state
props.description: Anything other than ready replaces the chart.

props.name: empty
props.description: What is missing, why, and an optional action. Shown in the empty state.

props.name: errorMessage
props.description: Message for the error state. A default says nothing was lost.

props.name: onRetry
props.description: Called by the retry button in the error state.

props.name: fallback
props.description: Shown instead of the chart when the frame is narrower than minWidth.

props.name: minWidth
props.description: Narrowest width in px at which the chart is drawn.

props.name: defaultView
props.description: Which view is shown first.

props.name: onDownload
props.description: Adds a Download data button and calls this when pressed.

props.name: stateHeight
props.description: Height in px of the loading, empty and error states, so the layout does not jump.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes on the figure.

examples.title: A chart with a summary and a table
examples.description: The summary says what the chart shows. View as table swaps the chart for the same numbers in a table.

examples.title: Loading, nothing to show, and a problem
examples.description: Loading shows a grey placeholder. When there is nothing to show, it says what is missing, why and what to do. A problem offers a retry.

examples.title: A tiny version in narrow spaces
examples.description: This box is too narrow for a full chart, so it shows a tiny trend line. The table view still has every value.

components.name: DataTable

states.name: focus
states.note: The scrollable table region can be focused with the keyboard and shows a focus ring.

states.name: sticky header
states.note: Pass stickyHeader (with maxHeight) to keep the column headings in view while the body scrolls.

states.name: scrolling
states.note: A table wider or taller than its box scrolls inside it instead of stretching the page.

states.name: empty
states.note: With no rows, a single line (emptyText, "No rows." by default) is shown under the headings.

states.name: sorted
states.note: A sortable heading (sortable on the column) cycles none, ascending, descending when pressed; the table shows arrows and says how it is sorted.

states.name: dense
states.note: Pass density="dense" for tighter rows.

states.name: up or down
states.note: A column's direction function adds an arrow and the up or down colour to a cell.

states.name: current row
states.note: The row matching activeRowKey is marked with aria-current and a sunken background.

states.name: row hover
states.note: When onRowClick is set, rows highlight on hover and the row name is a button.

components.summary: The numbers behind a chart, in a plain table with digits lined up.
components.description: DataTable shows numbers as a table. The first column names each row. Numbers line up on the right so they are easy to compare. Headings can sort, a cell can carry an up or down marker, and rows can be dense for screens people read all day. On a narrow screen the table scrolls sideways. ChartFrame uses it for the View as table view.
components.purpose: The numbers behind a chart, in a plain table. Numbers line up on the right with equal-width digits, so a column can be compared at a glance.
useFor: The table view of a chart, inside ChartFrame.
A small set of numbers that people need to read and compare exactly.
Giving every value that a chart shows only in a pop-up a place to be read.
A watchlist, a positions list or any list of numbers people sort and scan: turn on sortable headings, dense rows and the up or down marker.

notFor.text: Laying out a page or a form
A side-by-side comparison of products or plans
One headline number

whenToUse: Put the unit in each number column heading.
Use commas in big numbers and the same decimals down a column.
Include every number the chart shows, even ones that only appear in a pop-up.
Mark missing values with words such as "No data".
avoid: Don't line text up on the right.
Don't merge cells or stack headings. Keep one row of headings.
Don't use it to lay out a page. It is for data.
accessibility: It is a real table: the first column names each row, and screen readers pair each number with its headings.
The caption is read by screen readers and also names the scrolling area.
The scrolling area can be reached with the Tab key, so keyboard users can scroll it sideways.
Number columns line up on the right with equal-width digits.
A sortable heading is a real button inside the heading cell. The heading carries aria-sort, and a polite message says how the table is now sorted.
An up or down marker has an arrow shape and a hidden word, so direction is not colour alone.
When rows can be chosen, the row name is a real button and the chosen row has aria-current.
accessibilityYouDo: Write a caption that says what the table holds. It is hidden on screen, and screen readers use it as the table's name.
Put the unit in each number column heading, so each number is heard with its unit.
Write missing values as words, such as "No data", not as an empty cell.
The up or down marker adds an arrow and a hidden word, but your text must still carry its own sign (+ or −). Do not leave the number unsigned and rely on the colour.
If you keep the sort in your own code, pass sort and onSortChange together, or the headings will look broken.
onPhone: By default the table keeps its columns and scrolls sideways inside its own box, so the page itself never scrolls sideways.
Set responsive="stack" and a narrow container turns each row into a card with the column name before each value, so nothing scrolls.
Sort buttons in the header and the first-column row button are 44px tall on touch screens.
Tapping anywhere on a row calls onRowClick, so there is no hover state to rely on.

props.name: columns
props.description: Column definitions: key, header, numeric, sortable, sortValue and direction. The first column is the row header. sortValue gives the raw number or text to sort by when the cell shows formatted text. direction returns "up", "down" or "flat" for a cell, which adds an arrow and the up or down colour.

props.name: rows
props.description: One object per row, keyed by column key. Values are already formatted.

props.name: caption
props.description: Names the table and states what it holds. It is also the accessible name of the scroll region.

props.name: stickyHeader
props.description: Keeps the header row visible while the body scrolls. Pair it with maxHeight.

props.name: maxHeight
props.description: Maximum height in px before the table scrolls vertically.

props.name: density
props.description: Row spacing. Dense fits more rows.

props.name: sort
props.description: The current sort, when your code keeps it. SortState is { key, direction: "asc" | "desc" }. Use with onSortChange.

props.name: defaultSort
props.description: The starting sort when the table keeps it itself.

props.name: onSortChange
props.description: Called when a sortable heading is pressed. Each press goes none, ascending, descending, none.

props.name: onRowClick
props.description: Called when a row is chosen. The row name becomes a button, so the keyboard works. Clicking elsewhere on the row also calls it.

props.name: activeRowKey
props.description: Key of the row to mark as the current one (aria-current). Matches rowKey.

props.name: rowKey
props.description: A stable key per row. Defaults to the row's id value, then its position. Needed for activeRowKey when rows reorder.

props.name: responsive
props.description: What a narrow container does with the table. scroll keeps the columns and scrolls sideways. stack turns each row into a card, with the column name before each value, so nothing scrolls. It follows the width of the table's own container, not the screen.

props.name: emptyText
props.description: Shown when there are no rows.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes on the scroll region.

examples.title: Wait times by shop
examples.description: Number columns line up on the right. Values are already formatted.

examples.title: A long table with fixed headings
examples.description: For long tables, headings stay in view while the rows scroll.

examples.title: Cards on a phone
examples.description: Set responsive to stack and each row becomes a card when the table is narrow, with the column name before each value. Nothing scrolls sideways. This frame is narrow on purpose, so you see the phone layout here.

examples.title: Sortable, dense, with up and down
examples.description: A watchlist. Headings sort (none, then ascending, then descending). The change column gets an arrow and a colour. Pressing a row name chooses that row.

components.name: StatTile

states.name: better
states.note: When the delta direction matches goodDirection, the change is shown in green with the word better.

states.name: worse
states.note: When the delta direction is the opposite of goodDirection, the change is shown in red with the word worse.

states.name: flat or neutral
states.note: A flat change, or goodDirection set to neutral, is shown in the muted colour with no verdict.

states.name: needs action
states.note: Pass needsAction to add an attention tag and turn the threshold bar to the warning colour.

states.name: threshold
states.note: Pass threshold to show a meter bar with a marker at the limit and its label below.

components.summary: One big number with how it changed, an optional tiny trend line and an optional limit.
components.description: StatTile shows a name, a big number and how much it changed. The change has an arrow, a plus or minus, and the word "better" or "worse", so color is never the only clue. You say which direction is good, so a drop in wait time reads as good. Amber shows only when a person has to act.
components.purpose: One headline number with how it changed. The change says "better" or "worse" in words, and you choose which direction is good, so a drop in wait time reads as good news.
useFor: A row of the few numbers that matter most, above the charts.
A number with its change since the last period.
A number measured against a limit or target, shown on a small scale.

notFor.text: A change over time that people need to read point by point
Comparing several amounts
How much of an allowance is used or left

whenToUse: Say which direction is good on every tile, so lower-is-better numbers read correctly.
Say what the change is compared to, such as the previous 7 days.
For rates from small groups, show the range or group size in the detail line.
Put one row of tiles above the charts for the numbers that matter most.
avoid: Don't use amber for a number that just got worse. Amber means a person must act.
Don't rely on color for the change. The arrow, the plus or minus and the word "better" or "worse" carry the meaning.
Don't draw a chart with one bar when a tile says it.
Don't add labels to the trend line. The tile's number and change say it.
accessibility: Each tile is a group named by its label.
Screen readers hear the change as a direction word, such as "up", then the amount and "better" or "worse".
The arrow is hidden from screen readers. Color only repeats what the words say.
The limit scale is a meter, read with the value and the limit's label.
accessibilityYouDo: Set goodDirection on every tile where lower is better, or a drop is called "worse".
Say what the change is compared to in versus, such as "vs previous 7 days".
Pass a trend line with decorative set, so screen readers do not hear the numbers twice.
onPhone: The tile fills the width of its container and the value breaks onto a new line instead of overflowing.
The sparkline stays at its own size on the right and the text on the left shrinks first.
Nothing in the tile needs hover or a tap.

props.name: label
props.description: Metric name in sentence case, without a trailing colon.

props.name: value
props.description: Formatted value, for example 1.24 s or $4.2K.

props.name: serif
props.description: Sets the value in the display style.

props.name: delta
props.description: text (signed, with unit), direction (up, down or flat) and an optional versus period.

props.name: goodDirection
props.description: Which direction of change is an improvement. Use down for latency, cost and error rate. Neutral shows no better or worse word.

props.name: detail
props.description: Visible line under the value, such as an interval and sample size.

props.name: spark
props.description: Slot for a Sparkline. Pass it with decorative set.

props.name: threshold
props.description: value, max, at and label. Draws a thin scale with a tick at the threshold.

props.name: needsAction

components.summary: A tiny trend line that highlights the latest value and can be read aloud.
components.description: Sparkline draws a small line and marks the latest value with a bigger dot. Optional dots mark the lowest and highest points. A screen reader hears the first, last, lowest and highest values. Inside a StatTile it is only decoration, because the tile already shows the number.
components.purpose: A tiny trend line with the latest value marked, for places with no room for a full chart. It has no axes or labels, so it always sits beside a number.
useFor: Beside a headline number, inside a StatTile.
A table cell or list row that shows a trend.
The fallback in a ChartFrame that is too narrow for the full chart.

notFor.text: A trend people need to read exact values from
The only place the numbers appear

whenToUse: Put it beside a number that gives the current value.
Cover the same time as the number beside it.
Use it in place of a chart that is too narrow to draw.
avoid: Don't add axes, grid lines or labels. Use a LineChart for that.
Don't let a screen reader read it inside a tile. It would repeat the tile.
Don't compare trend lines as if they share a scale when they do not.
accessibility: On its own, screen readers hear the label with the first, last, lowest and highest values.
With decorative set, it is hidden from screen readers.
The latest point is larger, with a ring that keeps it clear of the line.
accessibilityYouDo: Set decorative when the number beside it already says the same thing, such as inside a StatTile.
Give it a label and unit that say what it measures. Screen readers use them.
Put the full numbers in a table somewhere on the page.
onPhone: It is a fixed-size picture, 96 by 28px unless you pass width and height, so it does not resize with its container.
It has no hover or tap behaviour, so put the numbers next to it in text.
Set width yourself if you need it larger on a phone.

components.summary: A line chart for change over time. Lines are named at their ends and can be explored with the keyboard.
components.description: LineChart draws up to five lines. Solid lines are real numbers and dotted lines are guesses about the future. From the third line on, a dash pattern and a marker shape back up the color. With two to four lines, each is named at its end. You can tab to the chart and use the arrow keys to move between points.
components.purpose: Shows change over time for up to five lines. Lines are named at their ends where there is room, so people do not have to look back and forth at a key.
useFor: A measure tracked over days, hours or months.
Comparing a few groups over the same time.
A forecast after real values: set where the projection starts.
Live data where the latest point may still change: turn on streaming.

notFor.text: Comparing amounts at one point in time
A trend in a very small space
A best guess with a range

whenToUse: Use it for change over time. Keep to four lines where you can.
Use solid lines for real numbers and dotted lines only for forecasts.
Put it in a ChartFrame with a summary and a table.
Switch to several small charts when lines bunch up and their names would overlap.
Group extra lines into one "Other" line. Lines after the fifth are not drawn.
avoid: Don't put two different measures on one chart. Use two charts.
Don't add a sixth line. Group the smallest into one grey "Other" line.
Don't change the other colors when a filter removes a line. Each line keeps its color.
Don't use amber for a line. It is saved for things that need a person.
accessibility: You can tab to the chart. Left and Right move between points, Up and Down switch lines, Home and End jump to the ends, and Escape clears.
Each step is read out as line, time, value and unit, with "projected" or "provisional" added when it applies.
From the third line on, a dash pattern and a marker shape back up the color.
The pop-up is hidden from screen readers, because the same values are read out as you move.
The draw-in animation is skipped when people turn off motion in their system settings.
accessibilityYouDo: Put it in a ChartFrame with a summary and a table.
Give it an ariaLabel and a unit, so each point is read with what it measures.
onPhone: The chart measures its container and redraws at that width, so it fills a phone screen.
Touch or drag on the chart to show the tooltip. Vertical swipes still scroll the page, and the tooltip stays until you tap elsewhere.
The tooltip flips to the left of your finger past the middle of the chart, and axis labels at the edges are pulled inward so they are not cut off.
Give the chart a height of about 200 to 240px on a phone, and it never goes below 160px.

components.summary: Bars that compare amounts. Highlight one bar, or stack up to four parts.
components.description: BarChart compares amounts. Bars always start at zero. You can highlight one bar in the main color and leave the rest grey. A stacked version splits each bar into up to four parts, with a key in the same order.
components.purpose: Compares amounts with bars that always start at zero. One bar can be highlighted while the rest stay grey, so the bar that tells the story stands out.
useFor: Comparing amounts across categories, such as shops or months.
Pointing at one category: set highlight.
Showing what an amount is made of, with up to four stacked parts.

notFor.text: Change over time across many points
A single number
A best guess with a range

whenToUse: Start every bar at zero. Never cut the scale.
Highlight a bar when it is the story, and leave the rest grey.
Lay bars sideways for long names or more than a handful of bars.
Keep stacks to four parts, and list the key in the same order as the stack.
avoid: Don't give every bar its own color. One set of bars takes one color.
Don't draw a chart with one bar. Use a StatTile.
Don't squeeze numbers inside bars that are too small. They sit at the bar end, and the table has them all.
Don't use a pie or donut to show parts of a whole. Use a stacked bar.
accessibility: You can tab to the chart. Arrow keys move between bars and, in a stacked chart, between parts. Home and End jump to the first and last bar.
Each step is read out as the part or measure, the category, the value and the unit.
Stacked parts have a small gap between them, and the key names each part in stack order.
The pop-up is hidden from screen readers, because the same values are read out as you move.
accessibilityYouDo: Put it in a ChartFrame with a summary and a table.
Give it an ariaLabel, a measure and a unit, so each bar is read with what it measures.
onPhone: The chart measures its container and redraws at that width. Long category labels are shortened with an ellipsis to fit.
Touch or drag on a bar to show the tooltip. Vertical swipes still scroll the page, and the tooltip stays until you tap elsewhere.
Horizontal bars suit a phone best, because labels have room to the left and the chart grows downward.

components.summary: Shows a best guess and how sure it is, with a caption that explains the marks.
components.description: DotPlot draws one row for each result. A dot shows the best guess and a thin line shows the range it likely falls in. A caption above says what the dot and line mean and how many people or cases it covers. The numbers are printed beside each row when there is room.
components.purpose: Shows a best guess and the range it likely falls in, one row per result. A caption says what the dot and line mean, because a bare range line means little to most readers.
useFor: Survey or test results where how sure you are matters.
Comparing groups of different sizes: turn on showN.
Results measured against a target, with a reference line.

notFor.text: Amounts that should be compared by bar length
Change over time

whenToUse: Write the caption so a reader can say what the line means, how sure it is and how many people are behind it.
Show group sizes when groups are small or differ between rows.
Print the numbers as text, so no one has to read them off the scale.
When the question is how two things differ, show that difference directly.
avoid: Don't leave the range line unexplained. A bare line means nothing.
Don't treat overlapping lines as proof that two results are the same. They are not.
Don't show scores with no range and no group size. At least show how many were asked.
Don't cut a bar chart to fit a range. This chart marks positions, not bar lengths, so its scale can start above zero.
accessibility: The caption is shown above the chart and is also part of the chart's name for screen readers.
You can tab to the chart. Arrow keys move between rows, and Home and End jump to the first and last.
Each row is read out as measure, row, value and unit, then the range and group size.
The range line has end caps, and the dot has a ring that keeps it clear.
accessibilityYouDo: Write a caption that says what the dot and line mean and how many people are behind them. Screen readers hear it as part of the chart's name.
Set measure, intervalLabel and unit, so each row is read in full.
Put it in a ChartFrame with a table. The numbers beside each row are dropped when the chart is narrow.
onPhone: The chart measures its container and redraws at that width. Long row labels are shortened with an ellipsis to fit.
Touch a row to show the tooltip. Vertical swipes still scroll the page, and the tooltip stays until you tap elsewhere.
The caption above the chart wraps, so write it in plain words.

components.purpose: A key that shows the same color, dash and marker as each line or bar, in the chart's order. It can also turn lines on and off.
useFor: One key shared by several charts.
A custom layout where the key sits apart from the chart.
Letting people show or hide lines: pass onToggle.

notFor.text: A chart with only one line. The title names it
A LineChart or stacked BarChart on its own. They draw their own key

whenToUse: Show a key for two or more lines, and none for one.
Keep the key in the same order as the lines or stack.
Let a hidden line keep its color. Hiding one line must not recolor the others.
Hide the line in the chart when its item is turned off. The key only tells you through onToggle.
avoid: Don't color the name text. The sample beside it shows which is which.
Don't make the key the only way to tell lines apart. With four or fewer, name the lines at their ends too.
Don't add a key for one line. The title names it.
accessibility: It is a list named "Legend" by default, and every item has a written name.
With onToggle, each item is a button that screen readers hear as pressed or not, with the word "shown" or "hidden".
The color samples are hidden from screen readers, because the name says the same thing.
From the third item on, a dash pattern and a marker shape back up the color.
accessibilityYouDo: List items in the same order as the chart's lines or stack.
Give it a label that says which chart it belongs to when a page has more than one key.
onPhone: The legend wraps onto more lines when the chart is narrow.
When the items are toggle buttons they are 24px tall. On touch screens they keep that size and have a 44px tap area.

components.name: Stack
components.summary: Stacks things top to bottom with an even space between them.
components.description: Stack puts items in a column with the same space between each. A tighter area shrinks the space on its own. Use it instead of adding space to each item by hand.
components.purpose: Puts things in a column with one even gap between them. The gap belongs to the stack, not to each item, so spacing stays consistent and shrinks in tighter areas.
useFor: A column of cards, paragraphs or form fields that need the same space between them.
A list of items, rendered as a real list element.
Groups inside groups, with a smaller gap inside each group.

notFor.text: Items that sit side by side in a row
Items laid out in columns
Limiting how wide a page column gets

whenToUse: Use the space setting between items, not extra margins.
Leave more space between groups than inside them.
Use a real list when the items are a list.
Put stacks inside stacks for groups, with less space inside.
avoid: Do not add margins to items to adjust spacing.
Do not use spacing outside the set sizes.
Do not space unrelated areas the same as related items.
Do not use Stack for a row. Use Cluster.
accessibility: It adds no meaning of its own: it renders the element you choose.
As a ul or ol it is still announced as a list, even though the bullets are removed.
Items keep the order they have in your code, so screen readers and the keyboard follow what people see.

Set as to main, nav or section when the stack is a page area, so screen reader users can jump to it.
onPhone: Items stack in one column and fill the width of the container.

components.name: Cluster
components.summary: A row of items that wraps to the next line when it runs out of room.
components.description: Cluster puts items in a row and wraps them to the next line when space runs out. Use it for tags, rows of buttons and small details. It uses the same spacing as Stack.
components.purpose: A row of small things that wraps onto the next line instead of running off the edge. Nothing is hidden or squeezed, so tags and buttons stay readable at any width.
useFor: A set of tags or filters.
A row of buttons, such as Cancel and Send.
Small details in one line, such as a file count and a date.
A label at one end and an action pushed to the other.

notFor.text: Items that go top to bottom
Form fields or cards that should line up in columns

whenToUse: Use it for groups that can wrap, such as tags and filters.
Keep the space smaller than the space between groups.
Use a real list for a set of related links or tags.
Line up the text bottoms when text sizes differ.
avoid: Do not use it for form columns. Use Grid.
Do not force one line and hide what does not fit.
Do not count on the order changing when items wrap.
Do not put long paragraphs inside as items.
accessibility: It adds no meaning of its own: it renders the element you choose.
As a ul or ol it is still announced as a list, even though the bullets are removed.
Items wrap to the next line instead of overflowing, so nothing needs sideways scrolling when text is zoomed.
Wrapping keeps the order of your code, so screen readers and the keyboard follow the same order.
accessibilityYouDo: Set as to ul or ol when the items are a list, and wrap each item in li.
Set as to nav when the row is a set of links for moving around.
onPhone: Items wrap onto the next line when they do not fit, so a row of chips or actions never runs off a phone screen.
The gap stays the same, and buttons inside a wrapped row keep their size and have a 44px tap area on a touch screen.

components.name: Grid
components.summary: A grid that changes its number of columns to fit the screen.
components.description: Grid sets how many columns show at each screen size. The defaults are 4 columns on phones, 8 on tablets and 12 on large screens. Or set a minimum item width, and the grid fits as many items as it can. The space between items follows the page spacing.
components.purpose: Lays items out in columns that change with the screen size: 4 on phones, 8 on tablets and 12 on large screens. Or give a minimum width, and it fits as many items in a row as there is room for.
useFor: A page layout with a side rail and a main area.
A set of cards that should fill the row and wrap.
Content that needs one column on phones and more on large screens.

notFor.text: A row of tags or buttons that should just wrap
A single column of items
Comparing options feature by feature

whenToUse: Set columns for page layout and a minimum width for sets of cards.
Use one or two columns on phones.
Keep items in reading order.
Use the page spacing so gaps change with the screen size.
avoid: Do not move items so they look different from reading order.
Do not give items a fixed width.
Do not put grids inside grids more than two deep.
Do not use 12 columns on a phone.
accessibility: It adds no meaning of its own. The items inside carry it.
Columns drop as the screen narrows, so content stays readable without sideways scrolling.
It never reorders items, so screen readers and the keyboard follow the order of your code.
accessibilityYouDo: Keep the order on screen the same as the order in your code. Do not use column placement to move items around.
onPhone: Below 840px it uses 4 columns by default, so on a phone each item must span columns or it gets a quarter of the width.
With the min prop it fits as many columns as it can, and a single column on a phone if min is wider than half the screen.
The gutter is 16px on a phone and grows at 840px.

components.name: Container
components.summary: A centered column with a set width and margins on the sides.
components.description: Container limits how wide a column can get: chat, home, page or full. It adds margins on the sides that grow on larger screens. The widths are proposals to confirm.
components.purpose: A centered column with a maximum width and side margins. Long lines are hard to read, so the chat width keeps a conversation at a comfortable line length.
useFor: The conversation and the message box, with the chat width so they line up.
Settings and documentation pages, with the page width.
A home screen, with the home width.

notFor.text: Laying out columns inside the page
Spacing items in a column

whenToUse: Use chat width for the conversation and the message box so they line up.
Use page width for settings and documentation.
Use the main element once per page.
Let side margins grow on larger screens.
avoid: Do not put containers inside containers.
Do not hard-code widths in components.
Do not use full width for running text.
Do not let chat lines run past about 80 characters.
accessibility: It adds no meaning of its own: it renders the element you choose.
Side margins keep text off the screen edge at every size, unless you turn them off with flush.
The chat and home widths keep lines of text to a readable length.
accessibilityYouDo: Set as to main for the main area of the page, and use main only once per page.
Do not use the full width for running text, because very long lines are hard to read.
onPhone: On a phone it fills the width with a 16px side margin, and the width presets do not apply because they are all wider than a phone.
Use flush when content such as an image must reach the screen edge.
It adds no safe-area padding, so add that yourself where content sits against a notch or the bottom bar.

props.name: size
props.description: Max-width preset. chat 768px, home 680px, page 1120px, full uncapped.

props.name: flush
props.description: Removes the side margins for content that bleeds to the edge.

props.name: as
props.description: Element to render.

examples.title: Chat width
examples.description: This width fits about 70 to 75 characters a line at normal text size.

  <Stack>…thread…</Stack>
</Container>

examples.title: Page and home widths
examples.code:

<Container size="page">…</Container>

components.name: Reveal

states.name: entering
states.note: On first render it rises or fades in, with a small stagger set by index.

states.name: reduced motion
states.note: When the user prefers reduced motion, no animation runs and the content is simply shown.

components.summary: Makes new content ease into view, one after another.
components.description: Reveal eases content in with a small rise or a quick fade. Items in a group appear one after another, with the delay capped so the whole group settles in under half a second. For people who ask for less motion, it shows content at once. The timings are proposals.
components.purpose: Eases new content in with a small rise or a fade, so people notice what just appeared. In a group, each item starts a moment after the one before, and the whole group settles quickly.
useFor: A new answer or card that appears once.
A short list of steps or results that arrive together.
Small status text such as Saved, using the fade.

notFor.text: Text that arrives word by word as it is written
Placeholders while content loads
Content that changes every second

whenToUse: Use it on content that appears once, such as a new answer or card.
Keep groups to a few items so the wait stays short.
Use the fade for small status text.
Pair it with Stack so the layout does not jump.
avoid: Do not animate things that happen all the time.
Do not wrap content that changes every second.
Do not delay long lists item by item.
Do not animate error messages.
accessibility: When people turn off motion in their system settings, content shows at once with no animation.
Content is on the page from the start, so screen readers can read it before the animation ends.
It only fades and moves a few pixels up. Nothing flashes or spins.
accessibilityYouDo: Do not let the animation be the only sign that something changed. If people need to know, say it in words or announce it.
onPhone: It plays the same short fade or rise on a phone, and nothing about it depends on hover.
With reduced motion turned on in the phone settings, it shows the content with no animation.

props.name: variant
props.description: rise is opacity plus 6px of travel. fade is opacity only.

props.name: index
props.description: Position in a group. Delay is index x 40ms, held at the fifth item.

props.name: as
props.description: Element to render.

examples.title: One after another
examples.description: Each item appears just after the one before.
examples.code:
<Stack gap={2}>
  {items.map((t, i) => (
    <Reveal key={t} index={i}>{t}</Reveal>
  ))}
</Stack>

examples.title: Fade only
examples.description: Use the fade when you do not want any movement.
examples.code: <Reveal variant="fade">Saved</Reveal>

components.name: StreamingReveal

states.name: streaming
states.note: Set with the streaming prop.

components.summary: Text that appears as it is written, with each new word fading in once.
components.description: StreamingReveal fades in each new word from a faint blur as it arrives, in --dur-base on --ease-arrive. Words already shown never animate again. A half-written word waits until it is finished, so words appear whole. For people who ask for less motion, text appears at once.
components.purpose: Shows a reply as it is being written, fading in each new word once. Words already shown never move or fade again, so the text stays calm to read.
useFor: The text of an assistant reply while it streams in.
Any text that grows word by word from a live source.

notFor.text: Content that appears all at once
A whole reply with its avatar, cursor and actions
Showing the assistant is busy before any words arrive

whenToUse: Add words in place and let lines wrap on their own.
Pass text in at a steady pace, about 30 times a second at most.
Mark the reply as finished when it ends so the last word shows.
Let Message handle what screen readers announce.
avoid: Do not animate height or position.
Do not rebuild old words, which would replay their fade.
Do not add your own blur or slide on top of the built-in fade.
Do not slow the text down to show off the effect.
accessibility: When people turn off motion in their system settings, the text appears with no fade or blur.
A half-written word is held back until it is complete, so words never appear in pieces.
Words are real text, so selecting, copying and searching the page still work.
It announces nothing by itself, so screen readers are not flooded with every new word.
accessibilityYouDo: Put it inside Message, or another part that tells screen readers when the reply is complete.
onPhone: Each new word fades in from a faint blur in --dur-base (220ms) on --ease-arrive, and new words add to the end so the text does not jump as it streams.
With reduced motion turned on in the phone settings, the text just appears.

props.name: text
props.description: Text received so far. Pass the buffer, not a delta.

props.name: streaming
props.description: While true, a trailing partial word is held back until it is complete.

props.name: className
props.description: Class for the wrapping span.

components.name: JumpToLatest

states.name: hidden
states.note: When visible is false the button is not rendered.

states.name: new messages
states.note: When count is above zero the label changes to New messages and a lime count badge is shown.

states.name: hover
states.note: The button gets a soft background under the pointer.

states.name: focus
states.note: A visible focus ring appears on keyboard focus.

components.summary: A small floating button that takes you back to the newest message.
components.description: JumpToLatest floats over the conversation. It says "Jump to latest", or "New messages" with a count if messages arrived while you were scrolled up. Click it to go to the bottom.
components.purpose: A floating button that brings a reader back to the newest message after they scroll up. It only appears when they are away from the bottom, so the conversation never pulls them down against their will.
useFor: A long conversation where the reader has scrolled up to reread something.
Telling a reader that new messages arrived while they were scrolled up, with a count.

notFor.text: Reading out new messages as they arrive
A general action inside the page

whenToUse: Place it over the conversation, not inside the scrolling part.
Show it only when the reader is away from the bottom.
Scroll smoothly on click, or at once for people who ask for less motion.
When you send a message, show it near the top and let this button handle the rest.
avoid: Do not pull a reader down who scrolled up on purpose.
Do not show it at the bottom.
Do not rely on the count alone. Keep the label.
Do not use amber. Nothing here needs a decision.
accessibility: It is a real button with visible text, so screen readers say what people see.
The count is read after the label, with a short pause between them.
When people turn off motion in their system settings, it appears without the rise.
When hidden, it is removed from the page, so the keyboard never lands on it.
accessibilityYouDo: Use scrollToBottom from useStickToBottom as the click handler. It jumps straight down, with no smooth scroll, when people turn off motion.
Make the scrolling area reachable by keyboard, so people can scroll the conversation without a mouse.
onPhone: The button is centered at the bottom of its thread. It keeps its size and has a 44px tap area on a touch screen.
It sits 12px above the thread's bottom edge and ignores safe areas, so place the thread above the composer and the home bar.
A tap scrolls to the newest message, and your code decides when the button shows.

props.name: visible
props.description: Shows the pill. Usually !atBottom from useStickToBottom.

props.name: count
props.description: Unseen messages. Above zero the label switches to newLabel and shows the count.

props.name: onClick
props.description: Scrolls the thread, usually scrollToBottom.

props.name: label / newLabel
props.description: Visible text for each state.

components.name: KeyTakeaway
components.summary: A labeled box for the closing point of an answer.
components.description: KeyTakeaway sets the closing point of an answer apart from the rest. An icon and a text label make it stand out, so color is not the only clue. Keep it to one to three sentences.
components.purpose: Sets the closing point of a long answer apart, so a reader who skims still finds it. A visible label and an icon mark it, so it does not rely on color.
useFor: The one to three sentence conclusion at the end of a long answer.
A recommendation that follows from the facts above it.

notFor.text: Warnings, limits or errors
A whole overview with sources and feedback

whenToUse: Use it once, at the end of a long answer.
Write a full sentence that makes sense on its own.
Keep the label visible.
Put it after the facts it sums up.
avoid: Do not use it for warnings. Use Callout.
Do not repeat the whole answer.
Do not use several in one answer.
Do not hide the label.
accessibility: Screen readers hear it as a section named by its visible label, so people can jump to it.
The icon is hidden from screen readers. The label carries the meaning.
accessibilityYouDo: Write a label that makes sense on its own, because screen readers use it as the section's name.
Use only one per answer, so the named sections stay easy to tell apart.
onPhone: Fills the width of its container, and the text wraps inside the box.
The small label is 12px on a touch screen.

props.name: label
props.description: Visible label. Also the accessible name of the region.

props.name: children
props.description: One to three sentences.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes on the section.

components.name: Timeline

states.name: done
states.note: An event with state done shows a lime dot with a check.

states.name: current
states.note: An event with state current shows a dark filled centre in a ringed dot.

states.name: upcoming
states.note: An event with state upcoming, or no state, shows an empty ringed dot.

states.name: failed
states.note: An event with state failed shows a red dot with a cross.

components.summary: A top-to-bottom list of events with times and an optional status.
components.description: Timeline lists events in order. Each has a time, a title, and optionally a description and a status. The status shows as a marker shape and as words, so it is never color alone.
components.purpose: Lists events in the order they happened, each with a time, a title and an optional status. The status is shown as a marker shape and in words, so it never relies on color.
useFor: What an agent did during a task, step by step with times.
The history of an update or a long job, including a step that failed.
A short log of events a person may need to check later.

notFor.text: Live progress of steps that are still running
A flow with decisions and branches
Steps that have no times

whenToUse: Use it when the order in time matters.
Give each time a standard date value too.
Keep titles to a few words.
Show the status in words as well as the marker.
avoid: Do not use it for steps with no time. Use a numbered list.
Do not rely on marker color for the status.
Do not put long text in the title.
Do not animate the markers.
accessibility: It is a numbered list, so screen readers say how many events there are and which one you are on.
Each time is marked up as a time, and carries the exact dateTime you give it.
Each status is written in words. The markers and the connecting line are hidden from screen readers.
accessibilityYouDo: Give each event a dateTime in a standard format, such as 2026-10-03T09:40, so software can read the time.
Translate the status words with stateLabels if your product is not in English.
onPhone: Events stay in one column, and the time, title and state wrap onto more lines when they do not fit.
Nothing in it is tappable, so there are no touch targets to size. The small state labels are 12px.

props.name: events
props.description: Each event has id, time, optional dateTime, title, optional description and optional state (done, current, upcoming, failed).

props.name: stateLabels
props.description: Replaces the state text for localisation.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes on the list.

components.name: ComparisonTable

states.name: recommended column
states.note: Set badge on an item to tint its column and show the badge under its name.

states.name: narrow screen
states.note: Below the small breakpoint the table becomes one stacked card per item.

states.name: scrolling
states.note: On wider screens a table that does not fit scrolls sideways and can be focused with the keyboard.

states.name: item limit
states.note: Only the first five items are shown.

components.summary: Compares 2 to 5 things side by side. On a small screen, it becomes stacked cards.
components.description: ComparisonTable lines up items against the same features in a real table. On a small screen it shows one card per item with the same details. Screen readers get only one version at a time. A badge marks the recommended item in words.
components.purpose: Lines up two to five options against the same features so people can compare them at a glance. On a small screen it becomes one card per option, because wide tables are hard to read on a phone.
useFor: Comparing plans, models or products on the same features.
Pointing out a recommended option among a few choices, with a badge.

notFor.text: The numbers behind a chart
Picking one of a few options inside a control
Laying out a page in columns

whenToUse: Compare two to five items on the same features.
Keep cell text short.
Mark a recommendation with the badge text.
Write a caption that says what is compared.
avoid: Do not use a table to lay out a page.
Do not compare more than five items.
Do not show a winner with color alone.
Do not leave cells empty. Write a dash or a reason.
accessibility: It is a real table with a caption and column and row headings, so screen readers say which option and feature each cell belongs to.
On a small screen the table is hidden and only the cards are shown, so screen readers read one version, not both.
The recommended option is named by the badge text, not only by its tint.
The table can be reached by keyboard and scrolled sideways when it is wider than the space.
accessibilityYouDo: Write a caption that says what is compared. It names the table for screen readers and heads the cards.
Fill every cell. Write a dash or a short reason instead of leaving one empty.
onPhone: Below 600px wide it switches from a table to one card per item, with each attribute in a two-column list, so nothing scrolls sideways.
From 600px wide it is a real table that scrolls sideways inside its box if it is wider than the screen.
Only one of the two forms is shown at a time, so screen readers do not read the data twice.

props.name: items
props.description: Two to five items with id, name, optional subtitle and optional badge. Extras are ignored.

props.name: rows
props.description: Each row has id, label and values in the same order as items.

props.name: caption
props.description: Names the table. Used as the heading of the stacked cards.

props.name: attributeLabel
props.description: Header of the first column.

components.name: ProcessDiagram

states.name: node kinds
states.note: Set kind on a node to draw it as a start pill, step box, decision hexagon, end box or dashed attention box.

states.name: selected node
states.note: Focusing or clicking a node outlines it and shows its detail in the line below the diagram.

states.name: narrow
states.note: When the container is too narrow for one row, the nodes stack top to bottom.

states.name: focus
states.note: Each node can be reached with the keyboard.

components.summary: A flow chart of steps and arrows, with a written version for people who cannot see it.
components.description: ProcessDiagram draws steps left to right, or top to bottom when space is tight. Shape and label carry meaning: a pill starts, a hexagon is a decision, a double outline ends, and a dashed box with an exclamation mark needs a person. It also has a short name, a written description, a step-by-step list and a way to view the source.
components.purpose: Draws a short process as steps and arrows, where shape and label carry the meaning. It always comes with a written version, so people who cannot see the drawing get the same information.
useFor: Explaining how a request moves from start to result.
A process with a decision or a step that needs a person.
A diagram whose text source people may want to copy.

notFor.text: Events with times
Live progress of an agent's steps
A chart or picture that is not a flow of steps

whenToUse: Write the description first and draw the diagram second.
Keep labels to a few words.
Give each step a short sentence of detail.
Keep the source viewable and copyable.
avoid: Do not show meaning with color alone.
Do not draw arrows between distant steps. Neighboring steps only.
Do not use more than about eight steps.
Do not leave out the written version.
accessibility: Each step can be reached with Tab, and screen readers hear its number, kind and name, such as "2. Step: Plan steps".
Focusing or clicking a step shows its detail in a line below, and screen readers announce it.
A numbered written version lists every step and where it leads, and a key explains each shape in words.
Arrows are hidden from screen readers, because the written version says where each step leads.
The selected step gets a darker outline, not only a color change.
accessibilityYouDo: Write a label that names the diagram and says a full description follows.
Write a description in plain sentences that says what the diagram shows.
Give each step a one-sentence detail, because it is read out when the step is focused.
onPhone: When the row of steps is wider than the container, the diagram switches to a single vertical column.
Tap a step to read its detail below the diagram. Steps are 56px tall and 132px wide.
The text alternative and the view-source button stay under the diagram, and the button has a 44px tap area on a touch screen.

props.name: nodes
props.description: Each node has id, label, optional kind (start, step, decision, end, attention) and optional detail.

props.name: edges
props.description: Arrows with from, to and an optional label. Draw them between neighbouring nodes.

props.name: label
props.description: Short alt. Names the diagram and says the description follows.

props.name: caption
props.description: Visible caption.

props.name: description
props.description: Long description, visible to everyone.

props.name: source
props.description: Replaces the generated Mermaid-style definition.

components.name: DiagramFigure

states.name: source open
states.note: Pass source to show a View source button that reveals the source in a code block and changes to Hide source.

states.name: scrolling
states.note: A diagram wider than the figure scrolls sideways and can be focused with the keyboard.

components.summary: Wraps a diagram with a caption, a full description and a way to view its source.
components.description: DiagramFigure gives any diagram a short name, a visible caption, a full description and an optional written version. If you give it the source, it adds a View source button that shows text you can copy. ProcessDiagram uses it, and so can any chart or image.
components.purpose: Wraps any diagram, chart or complex picture so it has a short name, a visible caption and a full description. A complex picture needs more than one line of text, so the full description sits on the page for everyone.
useFor: A chart or drawing that needs more explanation than a short name.
A diagram made from text, where people may want to view or copy the source.
A picture that needs a written alternative, such as a numbered list of its steps.

notFor.text: A flow of steps and arrows
A decorative picture with nothing to explain

whenToUse: Name the diagram in the label and point to the description.
Show the full description to everyone.
Offer the source when the diagram is made from text.
Wrap charts and images that need more than a short name.
avoid: Do not hide the full description in a pop-up.
Do not repeat the caption in the label.
Do not wrap decorative images.
Do not rely on a hidden description alone.
accessibility: It is a figure named by your short label, with a visible caption.
The full description and the written version are ordinary text on the page, readable by everyone.
The View source button tells screen readers whether the source is shown or hidden.
A wide diagram scrolls inside its own box, which can be reached by keyboard, so the page never scrolls sideways.
accessibilityYouDo: Write a label that names the diagram and says the full description follows. Do not repeat the caption.
Write a full description that gives the same information as the picture.
onPhone: The diagram scrolls sideways inside its own box if it is wider than the screen, and the box is focusable by keyboard.
The padding is 16px on a phone and 20px from 600px wide, and the caption and long description wrap under the diagram.
The View source button has a 44px tap area on a touch screen, and the source code scrolls sideways inside its block.

props.description: Visible caption.

props.name: description
props.description: Long description shown on the page.

props.description: Text alternative, such as an ordered list.

props.name: source
props.description: Textual definition. Enables the View source toggle.

props.name: sourceLanguage
props.description: Language label of the source block.

props.name: children
props.description: The diagram.

components.name: TakeoverBar

states.name: status
states.note: Set with the state prop.

components.summary: A full-width bar that says who is in control: you, or the assistant.
components.description: TakeoverBar tells you who is in charge right now. When the assistant is working, it offers Take over. When you have control, the assistant is paused and does nothing until you choose Resume or Hand back. In watch mode it names the one step you are asked to watch. The status sentence is read out once when it changes.
components.purpose: Makes control of a shared screen obvious, so the assistant never acts while the person thinks they are in charge. It offers the matching way to change control, so people can step in and hand back without stopping the run.
useFor: Above a screen or browser the assistant is operating, so people can take over at any time.
Pausing the assistant while the person does a step themselves.
Asking the person to watch one sensitive step, such as a payment.

notFor.text: A question the assistant needs answered
Approving one action
A run going on in the background

whenToUse: Keep the bar visible for the whole run so it is always clear who is in charge.
Use the watch state only for steps that really need a person, such as payment or sign-in.
Say what the assistant is not doing while you have control.
Keep the buttons plain: Take over, Resume, Hand back.
avoid: Do not use amber for the working or you-control states.
Do not let the assistant keep acting while the bar says you have control.
Do not hide Take over in a menu.
Do not collect passwords or card numbers through the assistant.
accessibility: Screen readers say the status sentence when the state changes.
The icon is hidden from screen readers because the sentence says the same thing.
The watch state is shown by an eye icon and words, not by color alone.
All actions are real buttons, and they wrap on narrow screens.
After Take over, Resume or Hand back, keyboard focus moves to the first button of the new state.
accessibilityYouDo: Keep one bar on the page and change its state, instead of swapping in a new bar, so the change is announced.
Pass step in watch mode, so people hear which step to watch.
onPhone: The text and the buttons wrap onto two lines on a narrow screen, with the buttons on the right of the second line.
The buttons keep their size and have a 44px tap area on a touch screen.
Nothing depends on hover, and the status text is announced when control changes hands.

props.name: state
props.description: Who is in control. Decides the text and the actions.

props.name: step
props.description: The step to watch. Shown in the supervise state.

props.name: onTakeOver
props.description: Fires from Take over, in the working and supervise states.

props.name: onResume
props.description: Fires from Resume. The agent continues from where it paused.

props.name: onHandBack
props.description: Fires from Hand back, in the you-control state.

props.name: labels
props.description: Overrides visible text: youControl, youControlHint, agentWorking, supervise, superviseHint(step), takeOver, resume, handBack.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes on the root.

components.name: AgentQuestionCard

states.name: answered
states.note: Once answered (or when answer is passed), the card collapses to a summary line with a Change button.

states.name: sign-in
states.note: Set reason to sign-in to show a lock tag and a hint not to type secrets, and hide the free-text box.

states.name: agent decides
states.note: Let the agent decide and Skip close the question with a matching summary.

states.name: text answer
states.note: Send is disabled until something is typed in the answer box.

states.name: hover
states.note: An option button gets a stronger border under the pointer.

states.name: focus
states.note: Options and buttons show a focus ring, and focus moves to the card after an answer or Change.

components.summary: The assistant asks you a question in the middle of a task, with quick answers.
components.description: AgentQuestionCard is how the assistant asks for help instead of guessing. A small label says why it is asking: choose an approach, needs information, needs a sign-in, or confirm a risky step. You can tap one of two to four choices, type your own answer, let the assistant decide, or skip. Once answered, the card shrinks to a one-line summary. It uses amber because a person has to act.
components.purpose: The assistant stops to ask instead of guessing. A label says why it is asking, and quick choices, a typed answer, Let the agent decide and Skip mean the person is never stuck.
useFor: Asking the person to choose between two to four approaches.
Asking for a fact the assistant cannot find itself.
Asking someone to sign in, or to confirm a risky step, before the assistant goes on.

notFor.text: Allowing or denying one specific action
Agreeing to a whole plan before work starts
Suggested next prompts after a reply

whenToUse: Ask only when a wrong guess would cost the person time or money.
Write the question so it can be answered without reading the log.
Give two to four choices that really differ, and say how in one line.

components.summary: One list of everything across your runs that is waiting for you.
components.description: NeedsYouInbox gathers every question, approval, failure and finished piece of work that waits on you, from all runs, in one place. Items are grouped by how urgent they are. Each row names the run, says what is needed, shows how long it has waited and has one button. When the list is empty, it says so plainly. It works on a phone.
components.purpose: One place for everything, across all runs, that is waiting on a person, sorted by how soon it needs them. Each row has one clear action, so people can clear the list quickly, even on a phone.
useFor: A home screen or side panel that collects questions, approvals, failures and finished work from many runs.
A phone view where people sort out what waits on them.
Saying plainly that nothing is waiting.

notFor.text: Every task, including ones that need nothing from the person
A single question inside a run
A catch-up when someone returns to one run

whenToUse: Sort by how urgent it is, then by how long it has waited.
Give each row one clear action.
Show the run name so people know where the item came from.
Use plain wait times such as 12 min or Yesterday.
avoid: Do not put finished-and-fine runs here. Only things that need a person.
Do not mark every group amber.
Do not hide the wait time.
Do not add extra actions to rows. Open the details instead.
accessibility: The inbox is a region named by its title, with real headings for the title and each group.
Each group is a list, so screen readers say how many items it holds.
Each button's name includes the run and what is needed, so the buttons do not all sound the same.
The type of item is written in words, not only shown by an icon or color.
Rows wrap on narrow screens.
accessibilityYouDo: Set headingLevel so the title fits the headings around it.
Keep actionLabel short, such as Answer or Review. The run and the need are added to the button name for screen readers.
onPhone: The card has 16px padding on a phone and 20px from 640px wide.
Each row wraps so the action button drops under the text, and long run names are cut with an ellipsis.
Action buttons keep their size and have a 44px tap area on a touch screen.

useFor: A row of background runs in a header or footer.
Opening a run's details or a quick peek.
Drawing attention to a background run that is waiting on the person.

notFor.text: A full list of runs with summaries and replies
Saying who is in control of the screen
A status that nobody needs to press

Open a peek or panel with the full story on press.
Group chips that need you first.
avoid: Do not use amber for working, done or failed runs.
Do not put more than a name and a short status in the chip.
Do not use a chip for an action. It only opens details.
Do not let the elapsed time tick every second for screen readers.

Amber comes with the words Needs you and a question-mark icon, so it does not rely on color.

The full record of every action
A section that people open and close, with no recap
